analysis.one_liner: Lets states, not the EPA, run coal ash disposal permitting, blocking stricter federal rules and federal enforcement.
analysis.headline: The House passed the coal ash bill 265-155 on July 25, 2013, but the Senate never voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let states, rather than the EPA, run the permitting program for coal ash — the toxic residue left after coal is burned at power plants. It sets first-time federal minimum standards like engineer inspections, groundwater monitoring, and dust controls, but also sets long compliance deadlines, bars the EPA from enforcing alongside states, and prohibits the EPA from ever finalizing its stricter 2010 proposed coal ash rule. The House passed it 265-155 in July 2013, but the Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal-fired electric utilities gain the most: the bill would replace the EPA's pending coal ash rulemaking with a state permit system, set compliance deadlines stretching as long as 84 months for existing ponds, bar the EPA from enforcing alongside states, and prohibit the EPA from ever finalizing its stricter 2010 proposed rule [S3] [S5]. Coal mining companies gain because the permit program could not reach coal ash placed at surface mining and reclamation operations [S5]. People near coal ash dumps would gain some protections that did not exist in federal law before, including engineer inspections, emergency plans for high-hazard ponds, groundwater monitoring, and public disclosure of monitoring data [S3] [S5].

how_it_helps.text: Creates the first federal minimum criteria for coal ash dumps in states that opt in, covering design standards, groundwater monitoring with corrective action, location restrictions in floodplains and fault zones, financial assurance, and record keeping.

Requires annual inspections of coal ash impoundments by an independent professional engineer, emergency action plans for high-hazard ponds, and immediate mitigation and notification of first responders when an inspection reveals a hazardous condition.
Requires new disposal structures to be built at least two feet above the water table and requires dust controls, with public access to permit documents and groundwater monitoring data.
Establishes a federal backstop: if a state declines to run a program or fails to fix deficiencies, the EPA must implement the permit program for that state.

analysis.who_pays: People living near coal ash ponds and landfills would bear the risk of slower cleanups and state-run enforcement with no federal backup, since compliance deadlines for existing impoundments stretched out as far as 7-8 years and the EPA could not enforce alongside states or finalize its own stricter rule [S3] [S5]. Utilities would pay compliance costs, but under timelines and standards largely set by the states where they operate [S5].

drawbacks.text: Compliance deadlines for existing coal ash impoundments stretch as long as 48 months for meeting core requirements and 78-84 months for final permits, and operators may keep running under existing authority the whole time.
The EPA is barred from concurrent enforcement whenever a state runs its own permit program, and may only assist if the state asks, so federal oversight largely ends in opt-in states.
The bill prohibits the EPA from finalizing its June 2010 proposed rule on coal ash, locking in the bill's own weaker framework as the ceiling on federal standards.
Coal ash used in surface mining and reclamation operations is expressly excluded from the permit program.

States get 6 months just to decide whether to participate and 36 months to certify a program, and federal takeover happens only if a governor opts out or the state fails to fix deficiencies after notice, so coverage of coal ash dumps depends heavily on each state's willingness to act.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have put some real protections into law where none existed federally — engineer inspections, groundwater monitoring, emergency plans, and financial assurance requirements for coal ash dumps. But its core trade was weaker oversight: long deadlines that could let unlined ponds operate for years, no federal enforcement alongside state programs, an explicit carve-out for mine-site disposal, and a flat prohibition on the EPA's stricter pending rule. The standards it created were also a floor states could exceed, while the bill blocked the higher federal standard from ever being finalized. For communities near coal ash ponds, the risk of slower cleanups and state-by-state enforcement outweighed the gains.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 265-155 in July 2013, and the Senate let it sit on its calendar until that Congress ended without ever voting on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 3, 2013, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and ordered reported on a 31-16 committee vote on June 19, 2013.
The committee reported the bill on July 10, 2013, and it was placed on the Union Calendar.
On July 25, 2013, floor amendments offered by Reps. Connolly, Waxman, and Tonko to strengthen the bill were debated and defeated, and the House adopted the committee's version.
A motion to recommit the bill with instructions to require wet disposal structures to prevent contamination of groundwater and drinking water failed 192-225, with all 225 noes cast by Republicans.
The House passed the bill 265-155, with 226 of 233 Republicans and 39 of 200 Democrats in favor.
The Senate received the bill on July 29, 2013, and placed it on its calendar the next day, where it remained without action through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People living near coal ash dumps came out ahead, because the bill died before it could lock in a state-run system with no concurrent federal enforcement and before it could bar the EPA from finalizing its own stricter coal ash rules [S5]. Coal-burning utilities avoided neither outcome for long — they did not get their preferred regime, but they also eventually faced federal rules rather than the lighter state-permit system this bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities near coal ash sites; EPA rules survived

sides.party_line_note: The House passed it 265-155 with 226 of 233 Republicans voting yes and 153 of 200 Democrats voting no; 39 Democrats crossed party lines to support it, and a Democratic amendment requiring groundwater protection failed 225-192 along party lines.

industries.note: The bill swaps the EPA's pending rulemaking for a state permit system with deadlines as long as 84 months, bars the EPA from concurrent enforcement, and expressly prohibits the EPA from finalizing its stricter 2010 proposed coal ash rule. Utilities would have kept operating existing impoundments under existing authority until those long deadlines passed.
The permit program cannot apply to the use, placement, or storage of coal ash at surface mining and reclamation operations, leaving that disposal route outside the new rules entirely.
